Baby & Child

Speech and Language Development in Toddlers

Updated: July 1, 2026

Language is one of the most astonishing things to watch develop: in about three years, a cooing newborn becomes a small person telling you a story about a dog they saw. The path from babble to sentences follows a fairly predictable arc , with plenty of individual variation , and everyday interactions with you are what power it.

From babble to first words

In the first year, babies work through coos, squeals, and then true babbling , repeated syllables like "ba-ba" and "da-da" , usually starting around six months. Late in the first year, babbling picks up the melody and rhythm of real speech, and gestures like pointing and waving appear.

First real words typically land around the first birthday, give or take a few months. Understanding runs well ahead of speaking at every stage: a one-year-old who says two words may understand fifty, following simple requests and turning at their name.

The toddler explosion: words to sentences

Vocabulary tends to grow slowly at first , many toddlers have somewhere around 20 to 50 words by 18 months , and then, often in the months after that, a naming explosion hits and new words arrive faster than you can count.

Around age two, most toddlers start combining words into two-word mini-sentences: "more milk," "daddy go," "big truck." By age three, many speak in three- to five-word sentences, ask endless questions, and are understood by familiar adults most of the time , even if plenty of sounds are still charmingly mispronounced.

These ranges are rough. Some brilliant talkers are late starters, and steady month-over-month progress matters more than hitting any single number on a chart.

Everyday ways to grow language

Children learn language from responsive back-and-forth with people , not from flashcards or apps. Narrate daily life ("We are putting on your red socks"), name what your child is looking at, and expand on what they say: when they offer "dog!", you return "Yes, a big brown dog is running!"

Reading together is the single most reliable language booster there is: books deliver rare words, repetition, and cozy one-on-one attention all at once. Songs, rhymes, and silly games do similar work.

The most powerful trick is also the simplest: respond. When a toddler points, babbles, or tries a word, treat it as a real conversational turn and answer. Then pause and give them time to reply , those serve-and-return exchanges are where language is built.

Bilingual homes: an advantage, not a delay

A persistent myth says two languages confuse children or delay speech. The research says otherwise: bilingual children hit major language milestones on essentially the same timeline as monolingual peers, and mixing languages in one sentence is a normal, clever use of their full toolkit , not confusion.

One fair caveat: a bilingual toddler’s vocabulary is spread across two languages, so counting words in only one language undersells them. Count words across both, and the totals are comparable.

So speak the languages of your home richly and without worry. Growing up bilingual is a lifelong gift , linguistically, culturally, and cognitively , and the best input is a parent talking naturally in the language they know best.

Red flags worth a conversation

Trust patterns, not single moments. It is worth talking to your provider if a baby is not babbling by around 12 months, has no words by 16–18 months, is not combining two words by age 2, or , at any age , loses words or skills they previously had. Not responding to sounds or their name, and few gestures like pointing by 12 months, also deserve a check (hearing is often the first thing tested).

If speech is very hard to understand at three, or your child seems frustrated by not being able to communicate, that is also a fine reason to ask. Raising a concern costs nothing: the answer is often reassurance, and when support like speech therapy is needed, starting earlier works better. "Wait and see" is the one strategy with no upside.

Key takeaways

  • Babble starts around 6 months, first words near the first birthday, two-word phrases around age 2.
  • Understanding always runs ahead of speaking , watch what your child comprehends, not just says.
  • Talking, reading, naming, and responding in everyday moments teach language better than any product.
  • Bilingual children develop on the same timeline; count their words across both languages.
  • No words by 16–18 months, no word combinations by 2, or any loss of skills , bring it to your provider early.

Frequently asked questions

My 18-month-old says only a few words. Should I worry?

There is wide normal variation, and many late talkers catch up , but no words by 16–18 months is worth mentioning to your provider. A hearing check and early evaluation cost little and often bring reassurance or timely support.

Do screens help toddlers learn to talk?

Language grows from live back-and-forth interaction, which video cannot replicate well for toddlers. A video call with grandparents is an exception because it is interactive. If your child does watch shows, watching together and talking about them adds real value.

Will speaking two languages at home confuse my child?

No. Bilingual children reach milestones on the same general timeline, and mixing languages in a sentence is a normal bilingual behavior, not confusion. Speak whichever languages you know best , rich, natural input in any language builds the foundation.
